newsitem.title: USA: Fed holds fire, US rates seen steady until yr-end.
newsitem.headline: Fed holds fire, US rates seen steady until yr-end.

text.p: The Federal Reserve kept U.S. interest rates steady on Tuesday, a decision seen by many as an indication that the central bank is growing more and more convinced that brisk growth and low-inflation can co-exist.
Analysts said they saw little evidence the U.S. economic outlook would change considerably in the near future, suggesting monetary policy could remain steady at least until November, maybe longer.

"The Fed did nothing today, and my guess is that they're not going to do anything probably through the end of the year," said Lawrence Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute, a Washington-based think tank.
The Fed left the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent at the year's fifth meeting of its policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
The central bank last tightened policy on March 25, when it bumped up the federal funds rate by 25 basis points. The Fed stood pat at its May, July and August meetings.
The Fed, captained by chairman Alan Greenspan, has shown the patience of Job and even a change in attitude when it comes to setting the course for U.S. rates, analysts said.

Greenspan, once seen as an inflation hawk, is now perceived as a central banker who believes productivity gains and greater global competition might foster economic growth without automatically triggering price rises, pundits said.

"The important thing for people to understand is that we can have this type of growth, or even faster, without causing inflation to accelerate," said James Medoff, an economics professor at Harvard University.
The U.S. economy grew at a moderate annualized rate of 2.2 percent in the second quarter from a torrid 4.9 percent growth pace in the first three months of the year.
Current estimates see Gross Domestic Product expanding between 2.5 and 3.5 percent in the third quarter. Meanwhile, consumer inflation has been quiescent at an annualized rate of around 2.2 percent.
Analysts said the current benign economic scenario reflects many factors, including stable and relatively low interest rates, a strong dollar and a consumer who is in good financial shape.

Also, experts said large corporate spending on capital goods has had a ripple effect on the economy, improving competitiveness and productivity on the one hand and keeping wage-inflation pressures under control on the other.
Wall Street crowned the Fed's decision with a 55-point rally on the Dow Jones Industrial Average to 7,860. The benchmark 30-year bond rose 5/32 to 98-8/32 to yield 6.51 percent.
But Wall Street pundits said blind faith in conventional wisdom could be deadly, adding that prudence was required before jumping on the "New Economy" bandwagon.

"The odds favor that there will be a tightening at some point. It's a tough call ... but I would say it slightly favors fourth quarter still," said William Dudley, chief economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc.
Dudley said he believed much of what would happen next to the economy depends on how the consumer behaved, adding that so far the fundamentals for U.S. buyers were "good enough."
